questions.stem: Why is emulsification called mechanical digestion rather than chemical digestion?

options.text: Because breaking drops into pieces changes no bonds or molecular structure
options.explanation: Correct — this matches the account taught above.
Bile salts are involved; the distinction is bond-breaking.
Bile is a fluid.

questions.stem: State where bile is stored before release.
questions.modelAnswer: Bile is stored in the gall bladder before it enters the small intestine.

questions.stem: Name the two products of lipid digestion by lipase.
questions.modelAnswer: Lipase breaks lipid down into glycerol and fatty acids.

questions.stem: Explain why emulsification speeds up lipid digestion.
questions.modelAnswer: Because splitting one large drop into many smaller ones multiplies the surface area on which lipase can act, and with alkaline conditions restored the enzyme works at its optimum, so glycerol and fatty acids are released faster.

questions.stem: A patient has their gall bladder removed. Predict the consequence for fatty meals.
questions.modelAnswer: Without the gall bladder's stored bile, bile still arrives from the liver but not in a concentrated bolus, so large fatty meals are emulsified less effectively and fat digestion proceeds more slowly and less completely.
